h1: Investor Renovation Contractor in Manchester, New Hampshire
intro:
Manchester's rental market is tight, and the reason is simple geography. It is the largest city in northern New England, an easy drive from the Massachusetts line, with no state income tax on wages and a housing stock that was built for the tens of thousands of people who once worked in the Amoskeag mills. Investors from Boston and southern New Hampshire buy West Side tenement blocks, inner-city three-families and post-war Capes here because rents hold up and vacancies stay short.

What makes Manchester deals go wrong is usually the building, not the market. Genstone Construction helps investors, lenders and servicers price that risk before they commit with a free Pre-Offer Rehab Review. After purchase, you get an itemized scope with labor, materials and draws, one field manager coordinating vetted, licensed local trades from our network, and permits and inspections handled with the city. You pay nothing at the start, draws follow completed work, and final payment comes after your approval.
housingStock:
Manchester was built around the Amoskeag Manufacturing Company, which at its peak ran one of the largest textile operations in the world along the Merrimack River. The mill complex still stands as the Millyard, now home to offices, tech firms and colleges, and the neighborhoods around it still show how the city housed its workforce.

The company built brick rowhouses and boarding blocks close to the mills, and some of that corporation housing survives near the Millyard and downtown. Beyond it, private builders filled the inner city and the West Side with wood-frame multifamily housing from the 1880s through the 1920s: three-deckers, side-by-side duplexes and the large three- and four-story tenement blocks that are a Manchester signature, many with flat or low-slope roofs and stacked rear porches. Rimmon Heights, Notre Dame and Corey Square on the West Side were the heart of the city's French-Canadian community, and their streets are still lined with these buildings. Bakersville, Hallsville and the inner East Side have similar stock.

The North End holds larger single-family homes, Victorians, Colonials and Foursquares built for mill managers and professionals, and it remains the city's most owner-occupied area. The South End and outer East Side filled in after the Second World War with Capes, ranches and raised ranches, and later with split-levels and some condominium complexes.

In the older buildings, expect balloon framing, lead paint, knob-and-tube or cloth-insulated wiring, galvanized supply lines, cast-iron drains and steam or hot-water heat, often with oil still in use. Flat-roof tenement blocks need careful attention to roof membranes, drainage and parapets. Foundations range from granite block and brick to poured concrete in post-war homes, and granite ledge is common enough to complicate excavation. Radon is a concern throughout southern New Hampshire, and testing belongs on every pre-purchase checklist.

commonIssues.title: Flat roofs on tenement blocks
commonIssues.body: Many of the West Side's three- and four-story wood tenement blocks have flat or low-slope roofs that collect snow, ice and standing water. Membranes reach the end of their life, internal drains clog and flashing at parapets and chimneys fails, sending water into top-floor apartments. Replacing the roof membrane, improving drainage and insulating the roof deck to cut ice formation are common capital items that come before any interior work upstairs.

commonIssues.title: Oil heat and aging boilers
commonIssues.body: Oil remains a common heating fuel in Manchester's older housing, often feeding a single boiler that serves every unit in a building. Old tanks, inefficient boilers and asbestos-wrapped piping are frequent findings. Converting to gas where service exists, separating heat by unit or adding cold-climate heat pumps can cut operating costs and improve reliability, and tank removal needs proper permits and disposal.

commonIssues.title: Lead paint in family rentals
commonIssues.body: Nearly all of Manchester's pre-1978 multifamily housing contains lead paint, and the city has many young families renting older apartments. New Hampshire requires lead hazard reduction when a child is found with lead poisoning in a rental, and the state has expanded childhood blood-lead testing. Building lead-safe window, porch and trim work into a renovation avoids reactive orders with tenants in place.

commonIssues.title: Radon and granite
commonIssues.body: Southern New Hampshire's granite bedrock makes radon a common issue in basements, and buyers, lenders and tenants increasingly ask for test results. Mitigation systems with a sealed sump and fan are a modest, routine line item when planned, and much more disruptive to add after finishes are in. Granite ledge can also complicate foundation repairs, drainage work and new sewer connections, which belongs in the budget.

commonIssues.title: Porches and second egress
commonIssues.body: Stacked rear porches and exterior stairs on three-deckers and tenement blocks often serve as the second exit from upper apartments. Snow load, ice and freeze-thaw cycles rot posts, loosen railings and heave footings that were never set below frost. Inspectors treat failing porches as life-safety issues. Rebuilding them to current code, with proper footings and connections, is a frequent permit item in Manchester multifamily rehabs.

investorMarket:
Manchester's investor market rests on demand that has outpaced supply for years. Healthcare employers such as Elliot Hospital and Catholic Medical Center, Southern New Hampshire University and the colleges in the Millyard, technology and financial firms downtown, and Manchester-Boston Regional Airport all draw workers, while the lack of a state income tax on wages pulls households from Massachusetts. Vacancy has stayed low, and rents have followed.

The West Side, including Rimmon Heights, Notre Dame and Corey Square, along with Bakersville, Hallsville and the inner East Side, is where most buy-and-hold and BRRRR investors focus. Three-deckers, duplexes and tenement blocks offer multiple units per lot, and renovated apartments rent quickly. The tradeoff is age: roofs, heating, porches and lead often need attention all at once.

The North End is the city's main owner-occupant market, with larger single-family homes that suit flips and high-quality renovations. Buyers here compare against Bedford and Goffstown, so finishes and systems matter.

The South End and outer East Side offer post-war Capes, ranches and raised ranches on larger lots, fitting first-time buyers using FHA or New Hampshire Housing financing and single-family rental investors.

Downtown and the Millyard have seen conversions of older commercial and mill buildings into apartments, which has added rental supply at the higher end but has not loosened the market for older multifamily units. For investors, the opportunity is strong rent demand paired with buildings that need real work. Accurate repair estimates before purchase are what separate profitable deals from expensive lessons.
permits:
Building permits in Manchester are issued through the Building Regulations division of the city's Planning and Community Development Department, which also handles electrical, plumbing and mechanical permits and inspections. Most work beyond cosmetic finishes needs a permit: structural repairs, roof replacement, porch and stair reconstruction, window changes that alter openings, plumbing fixture additions or relocations, electrical service upgrades and heating system replacements. Changes in use or unit count go through zoning review and sometimes the Zoning Board of Adjustment.

New Hampshire applies a state building code and state fire code based on the International Codes, enforced locally. Unlike Massachusetts and Connecticut, New Hampshire does not license general contractors, but electricians and plumbers must hold state licenses, and fuel gas and oil burner work requires licensed technicians as well. That makes vetting the general contractor's insurance and track record particularly important.

Manchester's housing code enforcement inspects rental units and responds to tenant complaints. The fire department enforces life-safety requirements in multifamily buildings, including smoke and carbon monoxide alarms, egress and fire separation, which are among the most common inspection items in tenement and three-decker renovations.
climate:
Manchester winters are long, cold and snowy, with temperatures well below what coastal Massachusetts sees and frost that drives deep into the ground. Footings for porches and additions need to sit below frost depth, and freeze-thaw cycles in spring and fall loosen masonry and heave anything that was set too shallow.

Snow load matters on flat-roof tenement blocks and on older pitched roofs with weak framing. Ice dams are common on poorly insulated buildings, so attic air sealing and insulation pay back quickly here. The exterior building season runs roughly from late spring into fall; roofing, siding, painting and porch reconstruction are ideally scheduled then.

The Merrimack and Piscataquog rivers can flood during spring thaw and heavy rain, affecting low-lying properties. Interior work runs year-round, but vacant buildings need heat or professional winterization, because burst pipes are among the costliest problems in vacant Manchester property.

faqs.q: Does Genstone have a Manchester office?
faqs.a: No. Genstone Construction's office is in Romeoville, Illinois. In Manchester and the surrounding towns, we coordinate a network of vetted, licensed and insured local contractors, and each project gets a designated field manager who handles scheduling, inspections and documentation. Investors who live in Massachusetts or farther away can follow progress through photos and milestone updates without driving up Route 3 or I-93 for every decision.

faqs.q: Why does contractor vetting matter more in New Hampshire?
faqs.a: New Hampshire does not license general contractors, so a company can start doing renovation work without a state credential. Electricians, plumbers and gas and oil technicians do need state licenses, but the general contractor running the job does not. Genstone vets the local contractors in our network for licensing where required, insurance and track record, and our field manager oversees the work so standards stay consistent from project to project.

faqs.q: Should I test for radon before buying in Manchester?
faqs.a: Yes. Radon is common in southern New Hampshire because of the region's granite bedrock, and buyers, lenders and tenants increasingly ask for results. A test during your due diligence tells you whether mitigation is needed. When it is, a sub-slab depressurization system is usually a modest cost compared with other rehab items, and installing it during the renovation is much easier than retrofitting after finishes are complete.

faqs.q: How do draws and final payment work?
faqs.a: There is no upfront payment. Your estimate includes a draw schedule tied to specific milestones, and money for each milestone is released only after the work is completed and documented with photos and, where the city is involved, passed inspections. Roll-off containers and hauling are built into the estimate. Lien waivers accompany payments, and the final invoice is paid after completion and your sign-off.

fix-flip.title: Fix and Flip Contractor in Manchester, NH | Genstone
fix-flip.metaDescription: Manchester, NH fix and flip renovations for North End homes and South End Capes: pre-offer repair estimates, radon and oil tank planning, buyer-ready finishes.
fix-flip.h1: Fix and Flip Renovations in Manchester, New Hampshire
fix-flip.intro:
Low inventory is the flipper's friend in Manchester. Buyers have had few move-in-ready choices for years, and a well-renovated house in the North End or the South End can draw strong interest quickly. That same demand, however, has pushed acquisition prices up, so the margin depends on knowing exactly what the renovation will cost before you bid.

Manchester flips also carry some regional quirks: oil tanks to remove, radon to test and mitigate, granite ledge under the yard and winters that compress the exterior building season. Genstone Construction prices those items in the free Pre-Offer Rehab Review, recommends a finish level that matches the neighborhood's buyer and runs the job with a single field manager and licensed local trades, keeping you updated without requiring a trip to the site.

sections.body:
The North End is Manchester's most established owner-occupant neighborhood, with Victorians, Colonials, Foursquares and Tudors on tree-lined streets. Buyers here often consider Bedford and Goffstown as alternatives, so a renovated North End home needs to deliver a convincing kitchen, updated bathrooms, refinished hardwood and systems that will not need attention for years.

Many of these homes still have original details worth keeping: oak and chestnut trim, built-ins, staircases and leaded glass. Preserving them while modernizing kitchens and baths is usually the surest route to top resale. Behind the plaster, though, you may find knob-and-tube wiring, old steam or hot-water systems, galvanized plumbing and minimal insulation.

Insulation and air sealing matter more in Manchester than in many markets. Buyers know about heating costs and ice dams, and an energy audit or a visible insulation upgrade can be a selling point. Two finish packages, priced side by side, let you pick the one recent North End closings actually justify.

sections.h2: South End and East Side: Capes and ranches
sections.body:
The South End and outer East Side are full of post-war Capes, ranches and raised ranches that sell to first-time buyers, many using FHA or New Hampshire Housing financing. These houses typically need kitchens, baths, flooring and paint, plus some combination of roof, heating system and electrical updates.

Oil heat is common, and buyers and insurers often prefer to see an old tank removed or replaced. Converting to gas where service is available, or adding cold-climate heat pumps, can become a selling point. Raised ranches often have finished lower levels that may show moisture or radon issues, so drainage, dehumidification and radon testing belong in the plan.

Post-war homes may contain asbestos in floor tile, duct wrap or siding, which must be tested and handled by licensed contractors before demolition. Buyers here want clean, durable finishes rather than luxury upgrades. Spending on systems and a solid roof, then choosing practical kitchen and bath finishes, usually produces the strongest return for this segment of the Manchester market.

Timing matters more in Manchester than in milder markets. Exterior work, including roofing, siding, painting, porch rebuilding and drainage, is ideally done between late spring and fall. A flip bought in November with a failing roof faces snow, cold and limited daylight before that work can be completed properly.

We plan around the calendar. When a flip closes late in the year, we prioritize getting the house weathertight before heavy snow, then focus on interiors through the winter with heat on. When it closes in spring, we push exterior work first to take advantage of the season.

Permits go in as soon as the scope is final, and we sequence trades so rough inspections can be grouped. You pay for finished milestones only, and photos show you each one. At listing, you have permit records, inspection results, radon test results and lien waivers ready for buyers and their lenders. Spring listings tend to meet the most buyers.

faqs.q: Which Manchester neighborhoods suit flips?
faqs.a: The North End is the strongest market for higher-end flips because buyers compare it to Bedford and Goffstown. The South End and outer East Side work well for Capes and ranches aimed at first-time buyers. On the West Side and in the inner city, multifamily buildings usually sell to investors or owner-occupants using FHA financing. Our free Pre-Offer Rehab Review tests your projected resale value against recent comparable sales.

faqs.q: Do Manchester buyers care about radon results?
faqs.a: Increasingly, yes. Radon is common in southern New Hampshire, and buyers' inspectors and lenders often request a test. A house with a mitigation system already installed and documented test results removes a negotiating point. Installing mitigation during the renovation is straightforward, while adding it after finishes are complete can be more disruptive and expensive. We include the post-mitigation test result in the listing packet.

faqs.q: Should I remove the oil tank before listing?
faqs.a: Usually it is worth it. Many buyers and insurers are wary of older oil tanks, especially buried ones. Removing the tank and converting to gas or heat pumps can make the house easier to insure and sell. If you keep oil heat, replacing an aging tank and documenting its condition helps. We include tank work in the scope with proper permits and disposal.

brrrr.title: BRRRR Rehab Contractor in Manchester, NH | Genstone
brrrr.metaDescription: Manchester, NH BRRRR renovations for West Side three-deckers and tenement blocks: scoped for the refinance appraisal, separate heat and durable rental finishes.
brrrr.h1: BRRRR Renovations in Manchester, New Hampshire
brrrr.intro:
Manchester's low vacancy is what makes the BRRRR model attractive: a renovated apartment on the West Side or in Hallsville will lease, and the rents support a meaningful refinance. The challenge is the building itself. Three-deckers and tenement blocks from the mill era often need their roof, heating, porches, wiring and lead hazards addressed all at once, and those shared items determine whether the appraisal lands where your refinance needs it.

Genstone Construction scopes Manchester BRRRR projects with the appraisal and the long hold in mind. Building-wide items and each apartment are priced on separate lines, finishes are chosen to survive tenant turnover, and documentation is assembled for the lender. Genstone Financial, a sister company, offers DSCR rental loans for the refinance step if you want them, though any lender receives the same package.

sections.h2: What moves a Manchester multifamily appraisal
sections.body:
Appraisers valuing a renovated Manchester multifamily look at comparable sales and at income. The items that usually move value most are visible and costly: a new roof (especially on flat-roof tenement blocks), updated heating with separate meters, rebuilt porches, an upgraded electrical service and renovated kitchens and baths in every unit.

Separating heat is particularly valuable here. Heating costs in a New Hampshire winter are substantial, and an owner-paid oil boiler serving six apartments is a large expense that reduces net operating income. Individual gas furnaces or boilers where gas is available, or cold-climate heat pumps, move that cost to tenants and can raise the value an income-based appraisal supports.

We price each element separately so you can see where capital will have the greatest effect on value. If the budget requires phasing, we help you prioritize the work an appraiser and lender will focus on first, then plan the rest after the refinance.

sections.h2: Rental-grade finishes for New Hampshire winters
sections.body:
Manchester tenants bring snow, salt and sand indoors for months each year, so flooring and entryways take a beating. Luxury vinyl plank handles moisture and grit better than carpet or laminate, and durable mats and boot trays at entries help. Washable paint with semi-gloss trim, laminate or solid-surface counters and widely available fixtures keep turns affordable.

Windows deserve attention. Old single-pane sashes in mill-era buildings are drafty and often carry lead paint on friction surfaces. Replacing them improves comfort, reduces heating costs and removes a major lead hazard in one step, which matters in a city where many tenants are families with young children.

Ventilation is the counterpart to tighter windows. Bathroom exhaust fans vented outdoors and kitchen ventilation keep condensation and mold in check during long winters with closed windows. We document the finish specification so future turns use the same products, keeping repairs fast and predictable across your Manchester units.

Lenders refinancing a renovated Manchester building usually ask for permit records, final inspections, before-and-after photos and proof that contractors were paid. Because New Hampshire does not license general contractors, lenders may also look harder at who did the work and whether licensed trades handled electrical, plumbing and heating.

We track permits through final inspection with the city, collect lien waivers with each draw and maintain a photo record of every phase. Electrical, plumbing and fuel work is performed by state-licensed technicians, and their information is part of the documentation.

When the project is complete, you receive a single package for your lender and appraiser: scope, permits, inspection results, photos, lien waivers and, where applicable, radon test results. If tenants occupied the building during the renovation, we record when each unit was finished so the rent roll matches the construction timeline. Underwriters in New Hampshire look for exactly that match when they judge whether income is stabilized.

faqs.q: Which Manchester neighborhoods fit BRRRR?
faqs.a: Investors commonly focus on the West Side, including Rimmon Heights, Notre Dame and Corey Square, along with Bakersville, Hallsville and the inner East Side. These areas have three-deckers, duplexes and tenement blocks with strong rental demand. The South End can work for single-family BRRRR plans. A Pre-Offer Rehab Review tests the specific building's condition, rents and comparable sales before you commit to a price.

faqs.q: Is converting from oil worth it on a BRRRR project?
faqs.a: Often. Oil heating costs in a New Hampshire winter are significant, and an owner-paid central oil system reduces net operating income. Converting to individual gas systems where service exists, or to cold-climate heat pumps, can shift costs to tenants and improve the property's income profile for both appraisal and DSCR qualification. We price conversion options alongside straight replacement so you can compare the long-term numbers.

faqs.q: Can the renovation proceed with tenants in place?
faqs.a: Yes. Many Manchester multifamily purchases come with some apartments leased, and keeping that income is usually smart in a tight rental market. We renovate vacant units first and rotate through the rest as leases end, scheduling heat and water shutdowns with notice and keeping stairways and porches safe. Lead-safe practices protect residents, many of whom are families with young children.

rental-renovation.title: Rental Property Renovation in Manchester, NH | Genstone
rental-renovation.metaDescription: Manchester, NH rental renovations: lead-safe work, housing and fire code readiness, winter-proof finishes and fast turns in a very tight rental market.
rental-renovation.h1: Rental Property Renovations in Manchester, New Hampshire
rental-renovation.intro:
With vacancy as low as it has been in Manchester, an empty apartment rarely sits for lack of tenants. It sits because it is not ready. The rental renovation question here is less about attracting renters and more about producing units that pass inspection, survive New Hampshire winters and turn quickly when a tenant leaves, all at a cost that fits your rents.

Our Manchester rental clients include owners of a single South End ranch, managers running dozens of West Side doors and funds holding condos across the city. We help you define a finish and systems standard that suits the climate and the housing stock, build code and lead requirements into each scope and plan turns so units are back on the market fast. Each job includes a written scope, a designated field manager and draws tied to completed work, with nothing due upfront.

sections.h2: A rental standard built for Manchester winters
sections.body:
A shared specification across your Manchester rentals keeps maintenance simple. Using the same flooring, paint, cabinets, counters, fixtures and appliances means replacement parts are on hand and future turns are easy to estimate.

The climate shapes the choices. Luxury vinyl plank stands up to snowmelt and road salt tracked indoors. Entry areas benefit from durable flooring and mats. Insulated exterior doors with good weatherstripping reduce drafts and heating complaints. In older buildings, replacing single-pane windows improves comfort and lowers heating costs.

Heating reliability matters more here than in milder markets. A failed boiler in January is an emergency. Where practical, individual heating systems per unit reduce the impact of any one failure. Ventilation is the other half of the equation: bathroom exhaust fans and kitchen ventilation keep moisture from building up in tightly closed winter apartments. We document the standard so future renovations and turns follow it consistently across your Manchester properties.

sections.h2: Code, fire safety and lead compliance
sections.body:
Manchester's housing code enforcement inspects rental units and responds to tenant complaints about heat, plumbing, electrical hazards, pests and structural conditions. The fire department enforces life-safety requirements in multifamily buildings, including smoke and carbon monoxide alarms, egress and fire separation between units.

We build those requirements into every renovation. That includes interconnected smoke and carbon monoxide alarms where required, secure stair and porch railings, GFCI protection, operable egress windows and heating systems capable of maintaining required temperatures through the coldest weeks of winter. In older buildings, we add fire blocking and address fire separation when walls and ceilings are opened.

Lead is a significant concern. Manchester has many young families in older rentals, and New Hampshire requires lead hazard reduction when a child is found with lead poisoning. Proactively addressing windows, porches, doors and trim during a renovation is far less disruptive than responding to a state order with tenants in place, and it protects both the tenants and your investment.

sections.h2: Faster turns in a tight market
sections.body:
In a low-vacancy market, every day a unit sits empty is lost rent that would otherwise be easy to collect. We like to see the apartment the week notice arrives, so the turn is priced and crews are booked before the tenant hands back the keys.

Paint, floors, repairs and the final clean are lined up back to back. Bigger finds, like a leaking tub drain or a porch post gone soft, get a same-visit price so the approval does not hold the next move-in.

Winter turns need extra planning. Snow removal, heating during the work and safe access for crews and materials all affect the schedule. We account for those factors so turns in January move as smoothly as turns in July.

Genstone Field Services, a company within the Genstone group, provides make-ready turns, inspections and occupied maintenance. Owners who use both get one coordinated team for routine turns and larger renovations, with consistent documentation across their Manchester properties.

faqs.q: Do you work with Manchester property managers?
faqs.a: Yes. Manchester property managers often bring us in at move-out, after a code complaint or when an owner approves a capital project such as a roof or heating conversion. Managers receive a scope they can forward, progress notes as work moves and a photo closeout to attach to the owner's file. Updates can go to the manager, the owner or both, which suits out-of-state owners.

faqs.q: What is excluded from the warranty?
faqs.a: For one year we stand behind the installation itself: if something fails because of how it was put in, it is ours to fix. It excludes tenant damage and normal wear and tear, which in Manchester rentals often comes from winter grit, salt and moisture. Choosing durable flooring, good entry protection and proper ventilation reduces those costs over time, and we can recommend a specification for your properties with that in mind.

faqs.q: Do you serve rentals outside Manchester?
faqs.a: Yes. Our network covers Manchester and nearby towns including Bedford, Goffstown, Hooksett, Londonderry, Derry and Merrimack, and extends into the Nashua area. Owners with properties across New Hampshire, Massachusetts and other states can use one specification, estimate format and reporting process for the whole portfolio, which simplifies budgeting and asset management. Nashua's mill-era multifamilies raise many of the same roof, heat and lead questions as Manchester's.

multifamily-renovation.title: Tenement & 2-4 Unit Renovation in Manchester, NH | Genstone
multifamily-renovation.metaDescription: Manchester, NH multifamily renovations for three-deckers, duplexes and tenement blocks: flat roofs, oil-to-gas conversions, porches and tenant-phased work.
multifamily-renovation.h1: Two- to Four-Unit Renovations in Manchester, New Hampshire
multifamily-renovation.intro:
The streets of Manchester's West Side, Bakersville, Hallsville and the inner East Side are lined with the buildings that housed the Amoskeag mill workforce: wood three-deckers, side-by-side duplexes and the larger three- and four-story tenement blocks, many with flat roofs and stacked rear porches. They are the core of the city's rental housing, and they share a set of renovation challenges driven by age, climate and shared systems.

Genstone Construction renovates two- to four-unit buildings across Manchester for investors, owner-occupants and funds, and scopes larger tenement blocks on the same basis. We price shared systems separately from unit interiors, plan phasing around tenants and handle permits, inspections and documentation for your lender.

sections.h2: Flat roofs, heat and shared systems
sections.body:
The most expensive items in a Manchester multifamily renovation are usually shared. On tenement blocks, the flat or low-slope roof carries heavy snow loads and is vulnerable to ponding, clogged drains and failed flashing at parapets and chimneys. A leak can damage the top-floor units and the framing below before anyone notices. Membrane replacement, improved drainage and added insulation are often the first priorities.

Heat is the second major shared system. Many buildings still rely on a single oil or gas boiler for every apartment, sometimes with asbestos-insulated piping. Separating heat by unit, using individual gas furnaces or boilers where service exists or cold-climate heat pumps, shifts costs to tenants and spreads the risk of a winter failure. Separate electric meters typically come with it.

We price these building-wide items apart from each apartment's interior. That gives you and your lender a clear picture of capital needs and supports phased renovation if budget or leases require it.

In a tight rental market, many multifamily buildings are purchased fully or partially occupied, and keeping that income is important. Empty apartments get done first; occupied ones follow as each lease runs out.

That requires careful planning in a cold climate. Heat cannot be shut off for long in winter, so boiler replacements and conversions are scheduled for milder weather when possible, or temporary heat is arranged. Water and power shutdowns are announced in advance and kept short. Stairways, porches and entries are kept clear of snow, ice and construction debris so residents can come and go safely.

Lead-safe containment and daily cleanup protect residents, many of whom are families with young children. Clear communication with tenants about schedules and access helps avoid conflicts and keeps the project moving. For owner-occupants, we usually complete their unit first so they can move in, then continue through the rental units with the same attention to safety and access.

Stacked rear porches and exterior stairs on Manchester three-deckers and tenement blocks often provide the second means of egress for upper apartments. Snow, ice and freeze-thaw cycles take a toll: rotted posts and ledgers, loose railings and footings that were never set below frost depth are common. Inspectors treat failing porches as life-safety issues, and rebuilding them usually requires a permit and, on taller structures, engineered details.

Inside, balloon framing and open stairwells can allow fire to spread between floors. Any time a Manchester wall or ceiling is open, the crew closes the floor-line cavities with blocking and brings unit-to-stair separations up to what the fire department will accept. Smoke and CO alarms are interconnected in every unit and the common stair.

The fire department's review of multifamily life-safety items is often the most detailed part of the inspection process. Planning these items from the start prevents delays at final inspection, improves insurability and makes the building safer for tenants.

faqs.q: Do you renovate larger tenement blocks?
faqs.a: Yes. While our core multifamily work is two- to four-unit buildings, Manchester's larger wood-frame tenement blocks come up often, and we scope them the same way: roof, heating, porches and electrical service as building-wide items, each apartment priced on its own, phasing planned around existing leases. Their flat roofs and larger heating plants call for specific trades, which our New Hampshire network provides.

faqs.q: Is separating heat worth it in a Manchester duplex?
faqs.a: In most cases, yes. With long, cold winters, an owner-paid shared heating system is a major expense, and a single failure leaves both households without heat. Individual systems with separate meters move costs to tenants and reduce disputes. Costs depend on gas availability, the existing system and building layout, and we quote separation alongside a single replacement for comparison. Heat pumps also add summer cooling tenants value.

faqs.q: Can I live in one unit while you renovate the others?
faqs.a: Yes. Many Manchester buyers purchase two- and three-family homes with FHA or New Hampshire Housing financing and live in one unit. We plan the renovation so your apartment stays livable, schedule shutdowns ahead of time and keep shared spaces safe, including snow and ice management on stairs and porches. Your unit is usually finished first so you can move in promptly.

fha-203k.title: FHA 203(k) Contractor in Manchester, NH | Genstone
fha-203k.metaDescription: Manchester, NH 203(k) renovations for owner-occupied duplexes, three-deckers and post-war Capes: itemized bids, consultant coordination and timed draws.
fha-203k.h1: FHA 203(k) Renovations in Manchester, New Hampshire
fha-203k.intro:
In a market with as little inventory as Manchester's, buyers who can only afford houses that need work have an advantage if they use the right loan. The FHA 203(k) program lets them purchase a dated South End Cape or a West Side duplex and roll the renovation into a single mortgage. With a two- or three-family, rent from the other units helps carry the payment, which is a strong fit for a city where so much of the housing is multifamily.

Genstone Construction is a certified FHA 203(k) contractor working with Manchester buyers, agents, loan officers and HUD consultants. We write bids that lenders can approve without repeated revisions, coordinate with consultants and plan the work around the draw inspections, flagging New Hampshire specifics like oil tanks, radon and winter scheduling early.

sections.h2: Limited or Standard for a Manchester property
sections.body:
For non-structural work up to $75,000, the Limited 203(k) is usually the right tool. In Manchester, that often means a South End or East Side Cape or ranch that needs a new kitchen and bath, windows, flooring, a heating conversion away from oil and lead-safe paint repairs.

Anything structural, or simply bigger, moves to the Standard 203(k), which carries the $5,000 minimum and brings in a HUD-approved consultant to write the scope and sign off each phase. West Side three-deckers and duplexes needing porch reconstruction, roof replacement, foundation repair or reconfigured layouts usually fall here, as do North End homes with major system work.

We walk the property early with the buyer or agent and separate structural from non-structural items. That lets the loan officer pick the right program from the start, rather than discovering after the consultant's visit that the scope does not fit a Limited loan. It also gives the buyer a realistic sense of the total budget before committing.

sections.h2: Manchester properties that fit the program
sections.body:
Owner-occupied two- and three-family homes are among the strongest 203(k) opportunities in the city. FHA allows one- to four-unit properties when the buyer lives in one unit, so a buyer can purchase a duplex in Rimmon Heights or a three-decker in Hallsville, renovate the whole building and use rent from the other apartments to help with the payment.

Those buildings commonly need what the program funds: heating replacements and conversions, electrical upgrades, porch reconstruction, roofs and lead hazard reduction. FHA requires deteriorated paint on pre-1978 homes to be corrected, which in Manchester's older housing is nearly always relevant.

Post-war single-family homes in the South End and outer East Side are also good candidates, especially those with original kitchens, oil heat and older electrical panels. A 203(k) lets a first-time buyer purchase and modernize these houses in one step. Radon mitigation, if testing shows it is needed, can typically be included in the renovation scope as well.

A 203(k) bid must give the lender and consultant line-item detail they can match against the work write-up. Ours lists materials, quantities, labor and a draw schedule in the lender's format.

After closing, funds move only when a consultant or lender inspector confirms a phase is complete. On Limited loans that pass the $15,000 inspection threshold, the same verification typically applies. We sequence the work so phases finish as inspections are scheduled, keeping crews moving and payments flowing.

Manchester's winters add a planning step. A 203(k) that closes in late fall with roof or porch work in the scope may need those items scheduled for spring, while interior work proceeds through winter. We build that timing into the draw schedule so the lender and consultant understand the sequence from the start.

City permits and inspections run in parallel, with lien waivers collected at each draw. Hidden conditions, such as rotted sills or failing drain lines, are documented and priced for approval before any work on them begins.

faqs.q: Can a 203(k) loan finance a Manchester three-decker?
faqs.a: It can, so long as one apartment is your primary home. FHA covers owner-occupied buildings of up to four units, and the renovation can include every apartment plus shared items like the roof, porches and heating. Larger tenement blocks with more than four units are not eligible. We scope the full building before you make an offer so your lender can size the renovation budget correctly.

faqs.q: Can a 203(k) cover converting from oil heat?
faqs.a: Yes. Replacing an aging oil boiler, removing the tank and converting to gas or cold-climate heat pumps are common 203(k) items in Manchester. Conversion depends on gas service availability and the home's layout. We price the options so the buyer and lender can choose before closing, and tank removal is handled with proper permits and disposal as part of the work.

faqs.q: When should a buyer's agent bring you in?
faqs.a: Before the offer, ideally. In a competitive market, buyers need to know quickly whether a house's needs fit their loan. A walk-through gives them a realistic repair range, identifies whether the work points to a Limited or Standard loan and flags items like radon, oil tanks and porch reconstruction that will affect the budget. That helps the offer stay realistic and the transaction stay on schedule.

reo-renovation.title: REO & Bank-Owned Renovation in Manchester, NH | Genstone
reo-renovation.metaDescription: REO renovation in Manchester, NH for banks, servicers and GSEs: freeze damage, flat-roof leaks, mold, code compliance and documented, option-based scopes.
reo-renovation.h1: Bank-Owned and REO Property Renovations in Manchester, New Hampshire
reo-renovation.intro:
A Manchester winter is hard on an empty building. When heat fails in a vacant three-decker or tenement block, frozen pipes and a snow-loaded flat roof can do more damage in a few weeks than years of occupied wear. Bank-owned properties here often arrive with burst plumbing, ceiling collapses on upper floors, mold in damp basements and porches that are no longer safe to use.

Genstone Construction handles REO renovation for banks, mortgage servicers, REITs, investment funds and the Government-Sponsored Enterprises that list us as a preferred contractor. In Manchester, asset managers get photo-documented condition reports, bids formatted for their systems, repair options tied to the disposition plan and vetted local contractors, with every step recorded for audits and investor reporting.

sections.h2: How winter damages vacant Manchester buildings
sections.body:
Freeze damage is the most frequent and expensive problem in Manchester REOs. Inland New Hampshire temperatures can freeze supply lines in exterior walls, unheated porches and basements within days of a heating failure. When the water thaws, it can run through several floors of a three-decker or tenement block before anyone notices, ruining ceilings, walls, floors and electrical systems.

Flat roofs on tenement blocks add another risk. Without maintenance, drains clog and snow accumulates; ice dams and ponding water find their way through failed flashing into top-floor apartments. In severe cases, roof framing can be damaged.

Mold follows water, especially in basements with granite or brick foundations that already hold moisture. Drying, remediation and stopping the source of water are typically the first work orders.

Vacant multifamily buildings may also see break-ins, copper theft and squatting. Each condition is photographed and described, which spares asset managers a trip north to see it.

Manchester's code enforcement staff respond to complaints about vacant and neglected property, including unsecured openings, accumulated debris, unshoveled sidewalks and unsafe porches. The fire department also takes an interest in vacant multifamily buildings because of the fire risk they pose to neighbors on tightly spaced West Side and inner-city lots. Unresolved citations bring fines and can stall a closing.

On each Manchester REO, we review the city's records for open violations and convert each one into a scoped repair: securing openings, porch and stair repair, debris removal, roof leak repair, smoke and carbon monoxide alarms. Permit-required items are filed, inspected and formally closed.

Winter adds a maintenance layer. Snow removal from walks and, on flat-roof buildings, from the roof itself may be necessary to prevent further damage and citations. Genstone Field Services, part of the same group, can provide preservation, inspections and winterization between initial securing and full renovation, keeping one team accountable for the property's condition.

sections.h2: Picking the repair scope for the exit
sections.body:
Manchester's tight housing market gives asset managers options. Multifamily buildings on the West Side and in the inner city often sell well to investors after securing, safety and code repairs, since buyers plan their own renovations and rental demand is strong. Single-family homes in the South End, East Side and North End may produce better recoveries after renovations that make them financeable for FHA, New Hampshire Housing or conventional buyers.

We price at least two paths: a minimum scope covering safety, security and code items, and a fuller renovation designed for owner-occupant financing. Asset managers can compare cost against likely proceeds and holding time, including the added risk of carrying a vacant building through a New Hampshire winter.

If tenants remain in a multifamily REO, heat, hot water and life-safety repairs take priority. Photos, a priced line for every item, a calendar and signed lien waivers travel with each Manchester bid.

faqs.q: Who assigns Manchester REO work to Genstone?
faqs.a: Asset managers at banks, mortgage servicers, investment funds and GSEs. We format bids for their approval platforms, offer a minimum and a financeable scope where that comparison is useful and send photo updates as work progresses. When a preservation vendor or listing broker is already assigned, we coordinate access and scope boundaries so nothing is duplicated, which matters on multifamily buildings where several vendors may be involved.

faqs.q: How do you handle a vacant building with a snow-loaded flat roof?
faqs.a: Safety comes first. We arrange for snow removal from the roof when loads are a concern, then inspect the membrane, drains and flashing for damage and leaks. Interior ceilings and framing below are checked for water damage and mold. Findings are photographed and priced, so the asset manager can approve emergency work immediately and the full repair scope after review.

faqs.q: Can you winterize a Manchester REO while repairs are pending?
faqs.a: Yes. Professional winterization, including draining plumbing and heating systems and adding antifreeze to traps, can protect a vacant building while the repair scope moves through approval. In some cases, maintaining temporary heat is a better option, especially in multifamily buildings with complex piping. We recommend the approach that fits the property and document it for the asset manager. Winterization is re-checked on each inspection visit.
